Abstract GNE myopathy is a rare recessive myopathy associated with inclusion bodies on muscle biopsy.

The clinical phenotype associated with mutations in the GNE gene is distal muscle weakness and wasting while the quadriceps muscle is preserved. Most of the current information on GNE myopathy has been obtained through studies of Jewish and Japanese patient cohorts carrying founder mutations in the GNE gene. However, little is known about GNE myopathy in Europe where the prevalence is thought to be very low.

We report the clinical, pathological, and genetic characteristics of GNE myopathy in Britain and for the first time highlight two common mutations in the Northern part of the United Kingdom as well as a broader spectrum of clinical phenotypes, including asymmetry of weakness at disease onset and slow disease progression with preserved ambulation over several decades. We also propose that the prevalence of GNE myopathy may be underestimated due to the frequent absence of rimmed vacuoles in the muscle biopsy. Chaouch et al. Introduction Page 2 GNE myopathy is a rare-inherited form of distal myopathy associated with inclusion bodies on muscle biopsy. In contrast to other forms of inclusion myopathies2–4, it is recessive in inheritance5, 6.

The phenotypic descriptions of GNE myopathy include hereditary inclusion myopathy (hIBM), quadriceps sparing myopathy, distal myopathy with rimmed vacuoles, and more rarely myopathy with facial diplegia or proximal weakness. Historical differences in nomenclature and classification may have led to an underestimation of the disease prevalence 7. Recently, the term GNE myopathy has been coined to encompass all these phenotypic subgroups.

The diagnostic criteria of GNE myopathy include myopathy of early distal weakness, onset in early adulthood, mild or normal serum creatine kinase (CK) levels, rimmed vacuoles and detection of 1418nm filamentous inclusions7, 8. Inflammatory infiltrates are rarely seen in GNE myopathy in contrast to the sporadic form of inclusion body myositis (sIBM)7, 9. A definite diagnosis is conventionally confirmed by evidence of compound heterozygous or homozygous mutations in the GNE gene.

We report for the first time the clinical, histopathological, and genetic findings of all the patients with genetically confirmed GNE myopathy, diagnosed through the National Specialist Commissioning Team (NSCT) service for limbgirdle muscular dystrophies at Newcastle. Methods Clinical assessment A total of 26 patients were recruited via the Newcastle MRC Neuromuscular Centre, Institute of Genetic Medicine, Newcastle upon Tyne. Genetic testing for GNE myopathy in the UK is only available through Newcastle as part of the NSCT.

Comprehensive clinical histories and neurological examinations were completed during follow-up clinic visits. All participants provided appropriate consent. Further investigations included serum CK levels, respiratory function (using spirometry), ECG, and neurophysiological studies.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed in 7 patients. Axial and coronal planes of the pelvis and lower limbs were obtained using a conventional T1weighted spin echo sequences. Muscle biopsies were performed in 20 patients, 2 patients had repeat biopsies.

Muscle histology was assessed by standard procedures including H&E staining and were processed for immunohistochemistry (IHC) and multiplex western blot (WB)1. Results Geographical and demographic characteristics Genetic testing in Newcastle became available in September 2010 and a total of 87 full GNE gene screens have been performed since. 64% of the 87 referrals were from England, 14% were from Northern Ireland and 13% were from Scotland.

The remaining referrals were from abroad. In total, 26 patients with GNE myopathy were identified, 12 females and 14 males from 23 kinships referred between 1987 and 2013. 10 of the 26 patients were from Scotland, 8 were from Northern Ireland and 7 from England.

1 patient was referred from the Republic of Ireland (figure 1). Based on our data, the point prevalence of GNE myopathy in Britain (England, Scotland and Northern Ireland) is 0.04 per 100 000 population. The point prevalence for Scotland is 0.19 per 100,000 population, Northern Ireland 0.44 per 100,000 population and England 0.01 per 100,000 population.

Of note the point prevalence of GNE myopathy in Japan is 0.3 per 100,000 population, one of the highest in the world. We accept that these figures need to be interpreted with caution in the absence of a more detailed population analysis and bearing in mind the challenges of disease ascertainment of GNE myopathy; however, it is worth noting that the estimated disease prevalence in Northern Ireland is close and possibly higher than in Japan. Clinical features The mean age of onset was 30 ± 9.238 years (range 1044 years).

14 patients presented in the fourth decade of life with two patients presenting in their fifth decade. The earliest age of onset reported was around the age of 10 years (table 1). Most patients presented with leg weakness (23/26).

Three patients presented with calf muscle wasting, difficulties playing football and tripping respectively. Most of those presenting with weakness had distal weakness (21/23). 23/26 were found to have either unilateral (9/23) or bilateral (14/23) foot drop at the first clinical assessment.

It is worth noting that all patients with unilateral foot drop progressed to developing bilateral foot drop.   Quadriceps sparing was evident at presentation in 21/26 patients and was still a feature at the most recent clinical assessment in 17 of these patients. Scapular winging was observed in 11/26 patients being asymmetric in 3 and symmetric in 8 patients and was noted at onset of disease in 4 patients.

Most patients remained ambulant (21/26) with 5/26 being wheelchair dependent. The nonambulant group was older with a mean age of 57.2 ± 3.513. 10 patients with a disease onset of 15 years or more retained the ability to walk.

Neurophysiological data was available for 14/26 patients. Myopathic features on EMG were seen in 11/14. Of the 7 patients in whom we had detailed EMG reports, the myopathic features were most evident in the anterior compartment of the distal lower limb, correlating with the clinical pattern of distal muscle weakness.

Neurogenic changes were reported in 3/14 patients. Muscle pathology reports were available in 20 patients. All biopsies showed at least mild myopathic changes except in 2, which were reported as normal or showed neurogenic features respectively.

Information on site of muscle sampling was available in 8 patients with the femoral quadriceps muscle being the most common site. In 3 patients biopsies were sampled from both the quadriceps and tibialis anterior muscles. Scattered cytoplasmic rimmed vacuoles/inclusions were identified in 5 patients only.

There was evidence of inflammatory infiltrates in 3 biopsies. Muscle MRI of the lower limbs was carried out in 7 patients (figure 2). Most images exhibited varying degrees of symmetrical muscle atrophy with relative sparing of the quadriceps in all.

Mutation analysis 21 patients were compound heterozygotes and 5 were homozygotes (in the absence of known consanguinity) with different GNE mutations (table 1). A total of 14 missense and 2 frameshift mutations were identified. Two frameshift mutations (c.805delG, Asp269Metfs*11 and c.1313dupT, p. Ser439Lysfs*6) and 6 missense mutations were novel (p. Ile618Thr, p. Gly393Glu, p. Asp111Tyr, p. Leu281Met, p. Gly86Arg and p. Val362Gly).

Of note, a previous pathogenic mutation (p. Val362Ala) was reported at the same position as our mutation p. Val362Gly10. Pathogenicity of the novel missense mutations was confirmed by parental testing showing segregation and/or in silico prediction tools (table 3). It is worth noting that 2 patients of Asian descent and a Northern English patient harboured the same heterozygous mutation (c.2179G>A, p. Val727Met).

Two previously reported mutations (c.1985C>T, p. Ala662Val and c.1225G>T, p. Asp409Tyr) were highly prevalent in the Scottish, Northern Irish and Northern English population. Both mutations were often found in the same patient in a compound heterozygous state. In 5 patients, mutation (p. Ala662Val) was found in a homozygous state.

Notably, these mutations were responsible for 33/52 pathogenic alleles (63%) in patients harbouring 2 mutations for the entire cohort, and 33/40 pathogenic alleles (83%) in patients from the North of the UK (Northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland). 90% (18/20) of patients from the North of the UK carried at least 1 of these mutations. We compared the clinical features of patients homozygous for p. Ala662Val (n=5) or compound heterozygous for p. Ala662Val and p. Asp409Tyr (n=10) with the remaining patients (n=11) and found no significant difference.

Discussion Page 5 GNE myopathy is an important diagnosis to consider in patients presenting with distal leg muscle weakness and elevated CK. This phenotype may be diagnostically challenging as it can mimic an inherited neuropathy or an alternative form of recessive distal myopathy like LGMD2B (Myoshi phenotype), caused by dysferlin mutations11, 12. The sporadic form of inclusion body myositis shares important pathological features with GNE myopathy, namely the presence of inclusions on muscle biopsy, but should be reasonably distinguished from the inherited form, based on the later age of onset, the clear preservation of quadriceps muscles in GNE myopathy and evidence of inflammatory infiltrates in the majority of sporadic cases of inclusion body myositis 9, 13.

We describe a sizeable GNE myopathy cohort which exhibits similarities to other previously reported patients with regard to age of onset, quadriceps muscle sparing and the progressive nature of the disease14–17. None of our patients developed respiratory insufficiency. The UK cohort is smaller than the previously described cohorts in Japan and Israel, and any conclusions are limited, but the clinical variability in both age of onset and progression appears to be greater in the UK.

We also note some asymmetry of weakness (unilateral food drop and scapular winging) at onset in several patients and slow disease progression. More than half of our patients with a disease duration of more than 15 years remained ambulant.   Both quadriceps sparing and asymmetry of muscle involvement were noted on muscle MRI and correlated with clinical signs.

Rimmed vacuoles, thought to be the hallmark of the condition, were only confirmed in a small proportion of patients. This may be related to the site of the biopsies sampled, with the quadriceps muscle being most frequently sampled and the least affected clinically (figure 3).   This, in addition to the distal and sometimes asymmetric presentation, may have led to a delay in diagnosis.

In our cohort, the mean delay in diagnosis from symptom onset was 17.21 years ± 11.91 years (range 353 years). With the introduction of genetic testing in the UK in 2010, molecular confirmation became more achievable leading to shorter diagnostic delays. Previous studies have indicated a possible association of homozygous kinase domain mutations in the context of early disease onset, and low level CK with a higher risk of respiratory failure18.

None of our patients developed respiratory insufficiency. One patient was reported to have mild systolic dysfunction and further investigations are awaited to ascertain its significance. Interestingly, the Northern Irish patients harbouring the p. A662V mutation exhibited a particular gradient of weakness in the distal deep finger flexors with more involvement of the index finger compared to the little finger in both hands.

To our knowledge, this is the first description of such selective muscle involvement in the distal upper limbs and seems to correlate with the genotype of the patient. More than 60 mutations in the GNE gene have been associated with muscle pathology5, 19– 21. In our cohort, mutation analysis revealed a number of novel missense (p. Ile618Thr, p. Gly393Glu, p. Asp111Tyr, p. Leu281Met, p. Gly86Arg and p. Val362Gly) and frameshift variants (c.805delG, Asp269Metfs*11 and c.1313dupT, p. Ser439Lysfs*6) spanning the J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry.

We have not identified any of the common mutations previously described in the Jewish and Japanese populations. Interestingly, we identified 2 very common mutations (c.1985C>T, p. Ala662Val and c.1225G>T, p. Asp409Tyr) in 18 out of the 20 patients diagnosed in Northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland; with 5 homozygotes carrying the c. 1985C>T, p. Ala662Val. 10 patients were compound heterozygotes for both mutations.

The c.1225G>T, p. Asp409Tyr mutation had previously been reported in 5 individuals: 2 from the United States, 2 from Scotland and 1 from Ireland10, 21. This is in keeping with the hypothesis that p. Asp409Tyr is a Northern British founder mutation. The c.1985C>T, p. Ala662Val mutation has previously been described in other populations of German, Irish, Jewish, American, Scottish, Japanese and more recently Chinese background5, 10, 16, 21, 23–25.

Therefore, this mutation may be generally very frequent or may have arisen several times in different populations. The predominance of these two mutations in the Northern British population is very striking and one should clearly consider a diagnostic strategy which may include early testing for the common GNE mutations in the UK and probably other parts of Europe. GNE encodes for a bifunctional enzyme (uridine diphosphoN-acetylglucosamine (UDPGlcNAc) 2epimerase/Nacetyl-mannosamine (ManNAc) kinase (GNE/MNK)) that catalyses the first two steps of sialic acid biosynthesis6, 8.

Sialic acid is the most abundant terminal monosaccharide on glycoconjugates in eukaryotes26. There are two distinct clinical entities associated with GNE mutations. The first is a metabolic disorder “sialuria” associated with excess sialic acid production.

The other disorder is GNE myopathy. It is worth noting that the functional impact of mutants on enzymatic activity and the inhibitory feedback system of sialic acid biosynthesis are key in determining disease manifestation. Indeed, GNE mutations in sialuria have been shown to impair feedback inhibition of the UDPGlcNAc 2epimerase by CMPsialic acid and may increase epimerase activity.

This is in contrast to the reduced enzymatic function seen in GNE myopathy for both kinase and epimerase domains. Complete loss of GNE expression is probably incompatible with life as evidenced by embryonic death seen with knock out inactivation of GNE in mice. In keeping with this hypothesis, all GNE patients identified so far carried a missense mutation at least on 1 of the mutated alleles, allowing for residual enzyme activity.

Remarkably in our cohort, 2 mutations seem to be very common: p. Ala662Val located in the kinase domain and p. Asp409Tyr positioned in the epimerase domain. Both these mutations have previously been reported and functionally characterised in vitro27, 28. Mutation p. Asp409Tyr was shown to result in a 60% reduction of epimerase activity and an 80% reduction of kinase activity while p. Ala662Val mutation displayed only slight reduction in kinase and epimerase activities.

In our patient cohort, patients homozygous for the Ala662Val had “milder” features with most presenting with unilateral foot drop and 4 out of 5 remaining ambulant after 3 to 19 years from disease onset. Transgenic mice expressing a human GNE mutation (Japanese founder mutation) were crossed with heterozygous GNE knockout mice to obtain Gne-/- transgenic hGNE D176V animals i.e. mice that express only mutant human GNE but no wild type mouse GNE29.

These mice show hyposialylation in muscle pathology after 42 weeks of age. Replenishing sialic acid metabolites was shown to prevent the disease phenotype in mice 30. Based on these observations, phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials using sialic acid or similar compounds have been initiated in the US and Japan

Any preliminary observation from these studies would need to be confirmed in larger cohorts. The success of these therapeutic trials will rely on a robust genetic diagnosis of GNE myopathy, accurate estimation of disease prevalence and the collection of relevant natural history data and appropriate outcome measures from diverse patient cohorts.
